Stay out of Excel Hell

​

One of the best ways to stay out of Excel Hell is to learn about what I like to call Modern Excel. The Excel of 20 years ago is not the Excel of Today. In particular, over the last 10+ years, Excel has made major enhancements. Below are just a few of the many features we have seen come to Excel since 2010.

​

  • Power Pivot
  • Power Query
  • Waterfall Charts
  • Dynamic Arrays
  • Data Types
  • LAMBDA’s
  • The Let Function
  • Office Scripts
  • Advanced Formula Editor Plug-In
  • Python
  • Group By and Pivot By Functions

Business Partners Corner

​

​

5 ways to hit the ground running when you have a new job at a new organization?

​

1. Meet with all stakeholders and LISTEN. Taking diligent notes and learning from your stakeholders (Finance, Non-Finance, Junior, Senior) is critical. For example, does the CEO or your Manager prefer high level information (one pagers) or detailed information?

​

2. Get out of your cube or office. I always encourage folks to visit stores, production facilities, customers and learn the business. This learning is game changing!

​

3. Learn the industry. Competitors, customers, key trends. Having an external view is a massive advantage, as many people are very insular. Having a fresh and well-informed perspective is important.

​

4. Study your P&L. When I was very junior, I witnessed a star performer at Kraft Canada who would lock himself in his office and study the current and historical P&Ls. When he emerged a week later, he asked great questions and quickly knew all his key metrics and the context behind business growth or decline.

​

5. Smile, be enthusiastic, be bold (after learning), and build a proactive 90-day plan. The First 90 Days by Michael D Watkins is a great and practical resource.

The FP&A Guy's Tech Tips

​

Below is a list of ten questions you should ask before starting the selection process for a new finance tool. Having a clear idea of why you need a new tool, what it will help you solve, and what is important in the way of requirements will increase your chances of success. Always make time to do your work upfront, and it will save you time and pay off in the end.

​

  • What is the main problem(s) to be solved?
  • What is the project scope? (financial planning, company-wide planning, etc.)
  • Make a list of all key stakeholders who should participate in the buying process and select a champion from the company leadership team to support the project.
  • Decide on all mandatory requirements for a new tool.
  • Perform an inventory of existing processes, reports, and budgeting/forecasting templates.
  • Decide on the budget for the project (annual, maintenance, implementation, training, etc.)
  • Determine the capabilities the tool will need today, in 1,3, and 5 years to support the business.
  • Review timelines for implementing the tool.
  • Determine who should lead the project and who are the subject matter experts.
  • How will project success be defined?

Ron's Recommendations

​

​

The Checklist Manifesto by Atul Gawande

I have never been as impressed with a book that had as mundane a title as a checklist! From start to finish, this was one of my all-time favourite books.

​

Atul Gawande is a graduate of Stanford and Oxford and went on to be a surgeon and a fantastic writer. He also has some fantastic TED & Google talks. Pretty impressive!

​

Atul’s noble quest was to reduce deaths and complications in surgery. He investigated the aviation and construction industries which both have brilliant safety records. The odds of being killed on a single airline flight was 1 in 29.4 million. The construction industry also has a brilliant track record compared to most industries.

The common factor was that both these industries had a discipline of using checklists to reduce avoidable human error. For example, Captain Sullenberger (Sully) landed a plane on the Hudson River after his plane encountered a flock of geese shortly after taking off. They used a checklist, and all 155 passengers survived this remarkable emergency landing!

​

So, Atul being somewhat underwhelmed tested checklists in hospitals around the world.

Despite tremendous skepticism that required significant change management, surgeons saw a dramatic improvement. Deaths fell by 47% and complications fell by 36%. Even a simple process like ensuring the right patient was on the operating table was often overlooked. They also implemented a process in which each person introduced themselves before surgery to each other, and this small initiative significantly reduced complications and improved teamwork.

​

So how the heck does this apply to Finance? Finance is not life and death, but this concept can have a massive positive impact within your team to reduce avoidable human error during chaotic processes or complex projects.

​

Using simple checklists for budgets, forecasts, and month ends, are three simple applications. Using a simple checklist can have a positive impact in a generally chaotic environment.

In my first role after University, I went from a low performer to a high performer in my first job when I implemented a simple formula (check) on my journal entry template to ensure it was balanced. This reduced my avoidable errors massively and was a significant turning point in my career.
​

A brilliant read with so many phenomenal and captivating stories from many industries. Checklists can be game-changers if used correctly and diligently!
